title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Kanagawa oki nami ura), also known as The Great Wave, from the series "Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku sanjūrokkei)"
creator: Katsushika Hokusai, Japanese, 1760-1849
medium: Color woodblock print; oban
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A crashing wave looms over two small ships, Mount Fuji in the background.
why: The best-known relief print in the world shows what carved blocks and flat color areas can achieve.

title: Woodblock for The Sparrow, from A History of British Birds
creator: Thomas Bewick, English, 1753-1828
medium: Wood engraving block
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A carved wood engraving block made by Thomas Bewick.
why: Showing the block itself makes clear that relief printing inks the raised surface left after carving.

title: Double-Sided Printing Block with Mongolian Script
creator: Mongolia
medium: Woodblock with black ink
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A double-sided wooden printing block carved with Mongolian script and still carrying black ink.
why: A text block from Central Asia shows that relief printing developed across many cultures and served words as well as images.

title: Saint Christopher
creator: Lucas Cranach the Elder, German, 1472-1553
medium: Woodcut in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black woodcut of Saint Christopher printed on ivory laid paper.
why: A European woodcut shows how carved black lines and white paper together build an image.

title: Roller Seal
creator: Olmec, Veracruz or Tabasco, Gulf Coast, Mexico
medium: Stone
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A carved stone roller seal made by Olmec artists.
why: An ancient roller stamp is a direct ancestor of classroom string rollers and shows a repeat pattern made by rolling.

title: Cylindrical Seal with Flower-like Motif
creator: Possibly Tlatilco, Valley of Mexico, Mexico
medium: Ceramic
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A ceramic cylindrical seal carved with a flower-like motif.
why: A cylinder stamp with a simple motif gives students a model for carving a pattern roller.

title: Stamp Depicting a Plant-like Motf
creator: Possibly Zapotec or Aztec (Mexica), Mexico
medium: Ceramic with pigment
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A ceramic stamp with a plant-like motif and traces of pigment.
why: A flat hand stamp from Mexico shows the same principle as a potato or foam stamp: the raised design carries the color.

title: Stamp
creator: Maya, Mexico or Guatemala
medium: Earthenware and pigment
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A Maya earthenware stamp with traces of pigment.
why: A second ancient stamp lets students compare designs and see how relief stamps were used two thousand years ago.

title: Nature Print of Moonwort and Adder's Tongue Ferns, plate 51 from The Ferns of Great Britain and Ireland
creator: Henry Bradbury, English, 1829-1860
medium: Nature printing, from an electrotyped lead plate, inked à la poupée, on off-white wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A nature print of moonwort and adder's tongue ferns on off-white paper.
why: Real ferns pressed into the plate show how nature printing records the exact texture of a leaf, the idea behind leaf prints and gyotaku, though this example used a lead plate.

title: Panel (Furnishing Fabric)
creator: Printed at Bannister Hall Print Works (English, active 1799-1840), Preston, Lancashire, England
medium: Cotton, plain weave; block printed
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A block-printed cotton furnishing fabric panel.
why: Block-printed fabric shows how a hand stamp is repeated across cloth to build an all-over pattern.

title: The Annunciation, from The Life of the Virgin
creator: Albrecht Dürer, German, 1471-1528
medium: Woodcut in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black woodcut of the Annunciation from Dürer's Life of the Virgin series.
why: Dürer's dense hatching shows how far carved line can go in a single black block.

title: The Lamb Receiving the Sealed Book, folio C from The Apocalypse
creator: Artist unknown, German, 15th century
medium: Blockbook woodcut hand-colored with brush, stencil and watercolor with additions in pen and brown ink on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A hand-colored page from a fifteenth-century German blockbook of the Apocalypse.
why: A blockbook page shows picture and text carved together on one block before movable type spread.

title: Triumph of Caesar
creator: Andrea Andreani (Italian, 1558/59–1629), after Andrea Mantegna (Italian, 1431–1506)
medium: Chiaroscuro woodcut from four blocks in black and light, medium and dark greenish gray on off-white laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A chiaroscuro woodcut of the Triumph of Caesar printed from four blocks in black and greenish grays.
why: A four-block chiaroscuro print shows how tone blocks are layered in register to model light and shadow.

title: Kanbara: Evening Snow (Kanbara, yoru no yuki), from the series "Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido (Tokaido gojusan tsugi no uchi)," also known as the Hoeido Tokaido
creator: Utagawa Hiroshige, Japanese, 1797-1858
medium: Color woodblock print; oban
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A woodblock print of a snowy black and white landscape of houses, trees and mountains, with three hunched figures in blue and yellow walking in the snow in the foreground.
why: A ukiyo-e landscape shows how Japanese color woodblock printing builds an image from separate color blocks.

title: Cancellation sheet, fragments of ten woodblocks from Intimacies
creator: Félix Edouard Vallotton (French, born Switzerland, 1865-1925), published by La Revue blanche
medium: Woodcut (ten separate blocks) in black on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A sheet printed from fragments of ten cut-up woodblocks from Vallotton's Intimacies series.
why: Printing the cut-up blocks to cancel an edition shows students how editions are limited and what a block looks like in pieces.

title: Two Women on the Shore
creator: Edvard Munch, Norwegian, 1863-1944
medium: Woodcut printed from one block (sawn into three sections) in dark blue, green, black and red-brown ink with additions in green crayon on cream Japanese paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color woodcut of two women on a shore, printed from one block sawn into three sections.
why: Munch's jigsaw method shows a simple way to print several colors from one block, and the wood grain is visible in the print.

title: Woodblock for The Urus or Wild Bull, from A General History of Quadrupeds
creator: Thomas Bewick, English, 1753-1828
medium: Wood engraving block
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A carved end-grain wood engraving block for Bewick's Urus or Wild Bull.
why: A surviving end-grain block shows the small size and fine engraved detail of Bewick's working method.

title: Woodblock for The Black Horse, from a General History of Quadrupeds
creator: Thomas Bewick, English, 1753-1828
medium: Wood engraving block
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A carved wood engraving block for Bewick's Black Horse.
why: A second Bewick block lets students compare the block with printed engravings of the same period.

title: The Night-Jar
creator: Thomas Bewick, English, 1753-1828
medium: Woodcut on ivory wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A small black-and-white print of a nightjar bird by Thomas Bewick.
why: Bewick's bird prints show the white-line technique, where the engraver cuts light out of a black block.

title: Book Illustration
creator: Thomas Bewick, English, 1753-1828
medium: Wood engraving on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A small wood engraving book illustration by Thomas Bewick.
why: A Bewick book illustration shows why end-grain engraving became the standard for printing pictures alongside type.

title: Colinet Mocked by Two Boys, from The Pastorals of Virgil
creator: William Blake, English, 1757-1827
medium: Wood engraving on off-white wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A small wood engraving by William Blake from The Pastorals of Virgil.
why: Blake's rough, expressive engravings show a different personality in the same tool and material.

title: The Major's Daughter, from "Once a Week"
creator: Joseph Swain (English, 1820-1909), designed by James McNeill Whistler (American, 1834-1903)
medium: Wood engraving on ivory wove China paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: Black ink print of a woman leaning on the side of a ship. She wears draped clothing and looks out, the sails' ropes behind her.
why: A magazine illustration shows the 19th-century division of labor, with one artist drawing and a professional engraver cutting the block.

title: Gutenberg Bible Leaf
creator: Johannes Gutenberg, German, c. 1398-1468
medium: Letterpress in black with initials in red and blue on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A leaf from the Gutenberg Bible printed in black with red and blue initials.
why: The first major book printed with movable type in Europe shows even, dense columns of letterpress text.

title: Colophon, from the Large Passion
creator: Albrecht Dürer, German, 1471-1528
medium: Letterpress in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A printed colophon page in black letterpress from Dürer's Large Passion.
why: A colophon shows how early printers recorded who printed a book and when.

title: Titles of Emperor Maximilian, from Historical Scenes from the Life of Emperor Maximilian I from the Triumphal Arch
creator: Written by Benedictus Chelidonius, German, c. 1460-1521
medium: Letterpress in black ink on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A page of black letterpress text on cream laid paper from the Triumphal Arch of Maximilian I.
why: A page of pure text lets students look closely at early metal type and spacing.

title: Philip Melanchthon
creator: Lucas Cranach the Younger (German, 1515-1586), block cut by Jakob Lucius (German, c. 1530-1597)
medium: Woodcut in black with letterpress on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A woodcut portrait of Philip Melanchthon printed with letterpress text.
why: Woodcut and type printed together show why relief images and metal type fit in the same press.

title: Portfolio Cover for Picturesque Views of American Scenery, No. I
creator: John Hill (American, 1770-1850), after Joshua Shaw, published by Matthew Carey & Son
medium: Letterpress on blue wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A letterpress portfolio cover printed on blue wove paper.
why: An early American cover shows display type and layout used for a title page, close to the look of a broadside.

title: Letterpress print (as companion to Doorframe, 2008.554)
creator: Artist unknown, American, 19th century
medium: Ink on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A nineteenth-century American letterpress print in ink on paper.
why: A 19th-century American letterpress sheet shows job printing from the era of wood type and hand presses.

title: The Etcher's Press - The Printmaker's Shop
creator: Abraham Bosse
medium: Etching on ivory wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etching of a 17th-century printmaker's shop with an etcher's roller press.
why: Shows the whole intaglio workflow, from inking and wiping the plate to running it through the press.

title: The Engraver and the Etcher
creator: Abraham Bosse
medium: Etching on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etching of a workshop showing an engraver and an etcher at work.
why: Contrasts the two basic ways of making an intaglio plate, cutting lines with a burin and drawing them for acid.

title: Street at Saverne copperplate
creator: James McNeill Whistler
medium: Cancelled copper etching plate
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A cancelled copper etching plate by Whistler.
why: Lets students see the actual metal matrix that intaglio prints come from.

title: Self-Portrait Etching at a Window
creator: Rembrandt van Rijn
medium: Etching, drypoint and burin in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A self-portrait print of Rembrandt etching at a window.
why: One print combines etching, drypoint, and burin, the three core intaglio line techniques.

title: The Map
creator: Mary Cassatt
medium: Drypoint in brown ink on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: Brown print on cream paper of two young female figures seated beside each other at a table, looking closely at a piece of paper.
why: Shows the spare, direct drypoint line in the hands of a major woman printmaker.

title: Portrait of James McNeill Whistler
creator: Paul-César Helleu
medium: Drypoint in black on pale blue laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A drypoint portrait of James McNeill Whistler on pale blue paper.
why: Shows the quick, sketch-like portrait drypoint and how burr gives lines a soft, velvety edge.

title: Whistler Asleep
creator: Giovanni Boldini
medium: Drypoint in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A drypoint of Whistler asleep.
why: Shows how a needle scratched straight into the plate can capture a fast, gestural sketch.

title: Mill Stream
creator: Donald Shaw MacLaughlan
medium: Drypoint in black on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A drypoint landscape of a mill stream.
why: Shows drypoint used for landscape, with rich dark accents from the burr.

title: Drypoint Number Five: Portrait
creator: Donald Shaw MacLaughlan
medium: Drypoint in black on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A drypoint portrait.
why: Gives a further example of drypoint line and burr in portraiture.

title: Saint George
creator: Martin Schongauer
medium: Engraving in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An engraving of Saint George.
why: Shows the crisp, swelling burin line and cross-hatching of early German engraving.

title: Erasmus of Rotterdam
creator: Albrecht Dürer
medium: Engraving in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An engraved portrait of the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam.
why: Shows Dürer's mastery of burin line for texture, from fur to paper to lettering.

title: The Prophet Amos
creator: Attributed to Baccio Baldini
medium: Engraving in gray-black on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An early Italian engraving of the prophet Amos.
why: Shows the fine-manner style of early Florentine engraving with delicate, closely laid lines.

title: Virgin and Child with Saint John
creator: Diana Scultori (after Raffaellino da Reggio)
medium: Engraving in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An engraving of the Virgin and Child with Saint John.
why: Work by one of the first women to publish engravings under her own name.

title: Portrait of Edouard Molé
creator: Robert Nanteuil
medium: Engraving on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An engraved portrait of Edouard Molé.
why: Shows the swelling, tapering burin lines of French portrait engraving.

title: Hyacinthe Rigaud
creator: Gérard Edelinck (after Hyacinthe Rigaud)
medium: Engraving and etching on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An engraved portrait of the painter Hyacinthe Rigaud.
why: Shows reproductive engraving translating a painting into systems of lines.

title: Ornament with Arabesques
creator: Daniel Hopfer, I
medium: Etching in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etched ornamental design of arabesques.
why: Comes from one of the first artists to etch for printing, a craft that grew out of decorating armor.

title: The Fair at Impruneta
creator: Jacques Callot
medium: Etching on two sheets of ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etching of the fair at Impruneta, printed on two joined sheets.
why: Shows how etching's fine, controlled lines can hold hundreds of tiny figures.

title: Black Lion Wharf, from A Series of Sixteen Etchings of Scenes on the Thames (the "Thames Set")
creator: James McNeill Whistler
medium: Etching with foul biting in black on off-white laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etching of a waterfront wharf on the Thames.
why: Shows freely drawn etched line and even foul biting, accidental acid marks on the plate.

title: View of Ponte Lugano on the Anio, from Views of Rome
creator: Giovanni Battista Piranesi
medium: Etching on heavy ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etching of the Ponte Lugano on the Anio river near Rome.
why: Shows dramatic tonal range built from deep and shallow bites of etched line.

title: A Painter-Etcher (Self-Portrait)
creator: Anders Zorn
medium: Etching on ivory wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An etched self-portrait of the artist.
why: Shows the bold, slashing parallel lines of late-19th-century painter-etching.

title: The Rialto
creator: James McNeill Whistler
medium: Cancelled copper plate
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A cancelled copper etching plate by Whistler.
why: Shows the etched copper plate itself, so students can compare matrix and print.

title: La Danse Russe (The Russian Dance)
creator: Jean-Baptiste Le Prince
medium: Aquatint with etching on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An aquatint with etching titled The Russian Dance.
why: An example from Le Prince, who helped develop aquatint to imitate wash drawings.

title: Chepstow Castle in Monmouth Shire, plate one from Twelve Views in South Wales
creator: Paul Sandby
medium: Aquatint with etching on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An aquatint view of Chepstow Castle.
why: Sandby popularized aquatint in England, and this view shows its soft, watercolor-like tone.

title: Francisco de Goya y Lucientes, Painter, plate one from Los Caprichos
creator: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes
medium: Etching and aquatint on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A self-portrait of Goya, the first plate of Los Caprichos, in etching and aquatint.
why: Shows aquatint tone laid behind etched line to model a face.

title: The Letter
creator: Mary Cassatt
medium: Color aquatint and drypoint on off-white laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: Print of a woman in a blue, patterned dress, seated at a desk and licking an envelope closed.
why: Shows flat color areas made with aquatint, inspired by Japanese prints.
check: The note that Cassatt inked her plates à la poupée comes from general knowledge; confirm it.

title: Afternoon Tea Party
creator: Mary Cassatt
medium: Color aquatint and drypoint, with additions in brush and gold, on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color aquatint and drypoint of an afternoon tea party, with touches of gold.
why: Another of Cassatt's color aquatints, showing color inked on plates à la poupée.

title: Laundresses Carrying Back Their Work
creator: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen
medium: Aquatint and drypoint, from a zinc plate, in black on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An aquatint and drypoint of laundresses carrying back their work.
why: Shows aquatint on a zinc plate with strong value contrasts.

title: Standard Bearer
creator: Prince Rupert of the Rhine (after Pietro della Vecchia)
medium: Mezzotint, with touches of engraving, in black on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A mezzotint of a standard bearer.
why: Made by Prince Rupert, who learned the new mezzotint method from its inventor, Ludwig von Siegen.

title: Lady Elizabeth Montagu
creator: James McArdell (after Sir Joshua Reynolds)
medium: Mezzotint on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A mezzotint portrait of Lady Elizabeth Montagu.
why: A classic English mezzotint portrait showing smooth tones scraped from dark to light.

title: Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire
creator: Valentine Green (after Sir Joshua Reynolds)
medium: Mezzotint on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A mezzotint portrait of Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire.
why: Shows how mezzotint reproduced the soft tones of oil portraits.

title: Prince Rupert
creator: Valentine Green (after Rembrandt van Rijn)
medium: Mezzotint in black on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A mezzotint portrait after Rembrandt.
why: Shows deep velvety blacks from the rocked plate with lights burnished out.

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows: the Rainbow
creator: David Lucas (after John Constable)
medium: Mezzotint with etching, in black, on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A mezzotint of Salisbury Cathedral seen from the meadows, with a rainbow.
why: Shows mezzotint used for dramatic light and sky in landscape.

title: The Genius of Lithography, from Alois Senefelder’s L’Art de la lithographie
creator: Nicolas Henri Jacob
medium: Lithograph in black on ivory wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black lithograph made as an illustration for Alois Senefelder's treatise on lithography.
why: It comes from the inventor's own book on lithography and introduces where planographic printing began.

title: Portrait of Senefelder
creator: Lorenzo Quaglio
medium: Lithograph on paper, printed from two stones
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A lithographed portrait of Alois Senefelder, printed from two stones.
why: It shows the inventor of lithography in a print made by his own process, using two stones for two tones.

title: Interior of the Lemercier Lithographic Printing House
creator: probably Charles Villemin and Victor Adam
medium: Lithograph from two stones on off-white wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A two-stone lithograph depicting the interior of the Lemercier lithographic printing house in Paris.
why: It shows a working nineteenth-century lithography shop, giving students a view of presses and printers at work.

title: The Lithograph Seller
creator: Nicolas Toussaint Charlet
medium: Lithograph in black on ivory wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black lithograph of a seller offering lithographic prints.
why: It shows how quickly lithographs became affordable everyday images sold to the public.

title: Nadar Elevating Photography to the Heights of Art, plate 367 from Souvenirs d’artistes
creator: Honoré Daumier
medium: Lithograph in black on white wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black lithograph by Daumier of the photographer Nadar, titled Nadar Elevating Photography to the Heights of Art.
why: Daumier's loose crayon line shows how drawing directly on stone keeps the energy of a sketch.

title: The Jockey
creator: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
medium: Color lithograph on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color lithograph of a jockey on horseback.
why: It shows how separate stones for each color combine into one image, with crayon texture still visible.

title: Zodiaque ("La Plume")
creator: Alphonse Mucha
medium: Color lithograph from multiple stones on tan wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color lithograph printed from multiple stones on tan paper, made for the magazine La Plume.
why: It shows the flat color areas and fine outlines that multi-stone poster lithography made possible.

title: Palais de Glace
creator: Jules Chéret, printed by Imprimerie Chaix
medium: Color lithograph on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color lithograph poster advertising the Palais de Glace skating rink in Paris.
why: Chéret's posters show how color lithography brought large, bright advertising to city streets.

title: The Bridge, from Some Aspects of Paris Life
creator: Pierre Bonnard, printed by Auguste Clot, published by Ambroise Vollard
medium: Lithograph on off-white China paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A lithograph of a bridge in Paris from Bonnard's series Some Aspects of Paris Life.
why: It shows an artist working with a master printer, Auguste Clot, which is how most artists' lithographs were made.

title: The Eye, Like a Strange Balloon Moves Towards Infinity, plate one from To Edgar Poe
creator: Odilon Redon
medium: Lithograph in black on ivory China paper, laid down on white wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black lithograph of an eye shaped like a strange balloon, from the series To Edgar Poe.
why: Redon's deep, velvety blacks show the rich tonal range a greasy crayon can give on stone.

title: At the Concert
creator: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
medium: Zinc lithographic plate with corners removed and beveled edges, laid down on mauve board and taped to mat
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A zinc lithographic printing plate with clipped corners and beveled edges, used for Toulouse-Lautrec's print At the Concert.
why: It is the actual metal plate an artist drew on, showing that lithography does not need a stone.

title: In Times of Harmony
creator: Paul Signac, printed by Tailliardat
medium: Color Lithograph in green, blue, yellow, red, and peach with scraping on plate, from a zinc plate on buff wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color lithograph in green, blue, yellow, red, and peach, printed from a zinc plate.
why: It shows a full-color print made from a zinc plate, with scraping used to bring back lights.

title: Design cover for West Point Song of the Graduates
creator: James McNeill Whistler
medium: Transfer lithograph in black on off-white wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black transfer lithograph designed as a cover for a West Point song sheet.
why: It shows transfer lithography, where the drawing is made on paper and moved to the printing surface instead of drawn directly on it.

title: Portrait of Ellen Andrée
creator: Edgar Degas
medium: Monotype in black and brown ink on ivory china paper perimeter mounted to a cream, laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A monotype portrait of the actress Ellen Andrée in black and brown ink.
why: It shows the dark-field method, where the artist wipes light out of an inked plate before printing one impression.

title: Landscape with Smokestacks
creator: Edgar Degas
medium: Pastel, over monotype, on textured cream wove paper, edge-mounted on board
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A landscape with smokestacks in pastel worked over a monotype base.
why: It shows how artists use a monotype as a starting layer and then add drawing media on top.

title: Tahitian Landscape
creator: Paul Gauguin
medium: Watercolor monotype from a glass matrix, with touches of gouache on cream wove paper laid down on ivory Japanese paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A watercolor monotype of a Tahitian landscape printed from a sheet of glass.
why: It shows that a monotype can be printed from glass using watercolor, a setup easy to recreate in a classroom.

title: Tahitian Girl in Pink Pareu
creator: Paul Gauguin
medium: Watercolor monotype from a paper matrix on cream laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A watercolor monotype of a girl wearing a pink pareu, printed from a paper matrix.
why: It shows a monotype pulled from a painted paper matrix, giving the soft blotted texture typical of the process.
check: Not yet viewed. Check the image is suitable for children before launch.

title: Street Scene
creator: Maurice Prendergast
medium: Color monotype on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color monotype of a street scene.
why: Prendergast's bright, painterly color shows the light-field method, where color is painted onto a clean plate and printed once.

title: Rookery Building, Chicago, Illinois, LaSalle Street Elevation
creator: Burnham & Root
medium: Multicolored hectograph print on heavy paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An elevation drawing of a multistory building with a large arched entrance and bands of windows, with a blue ground level and red detailing on the upper levels.
why: The hectograph, the ancestor of today's gel plate, printed copies from a tray of gelatin, and this example shows its multicolor results.

title: Victoria Hotel, Chicago Heights, Illinois, Front Elevation
creator: Adler and Sullivan
medium: Blackline and color Hectograph prints on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A front elevation of the Victoria Hotel in blackline and color hectograph prints on paper.
why: It shows how architects used gelatin hectographs to make several copies of a drawing before photocopiers existed.

title: Women's Temple Building, Chicago, Illinois, Ninth Floor Plan
creator: Burnham and Root
medium: Purple and red hectograph ink on linen
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A floor plan of the Women's Temple Building printed in purple and red hectograph ink on linen.
why: The purple aniline ink is the hallmark of hectograph printing from a gelatin pad.

title: Ottawa Opera House, Ottawa, Illinois, Wall Stencil Design
creator: Peter Bonnett Wight (American, 1838–1925)
medium: Gouache on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A gouache design on paper for a decorative wall stencil for the Ottawa Opera House in Illinois.
why: Shows how a repeating stencil pattern is planned on paper before it is cut and applied to a wall.

title: Furoshiki (Wrapping Cloth)
creator: Japan
medium: Wool, plain weave; resist dyed and stenciled (yûzenzome)
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A Japanese wool wrapping cloth patterned with resist dyeing and stenciling.
why: Shows that stencils print on cloth as well as paper, here through a Japanese stencil-resist dyeing technique.

title: A Condolence Card
creator: Emily Wilcox (American, 19th century)
medium: Stencil in black on buff wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A small card with a design stenciled in black on buff paper.
why: A simple one-color stencil on paper, close to what students make in a first stencil lesson.

title: The Arrival in France of Saint Francis of Paola
creator: Artist unknown (French, Toulouse, active c. 1495)
medium: Woodcut in gray, hand-colored with brush, stencil and watercolor on ivory laid paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A gray woodcut of Saint Francis of Paola arriving in France, colored by brush and stencil.
why: Shows that stencils were used more than 500 years ago to add color quickly to printed pictures.

title: Stencil with Design of Mallows
creator: Japan
medium: Mulberry paper treated with persimmon juice, with silk web reinforcement
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A Japanese paper stencil cut with a design of mallow flowers.
why: A real katagami stencil, showing the cut paper itself and the silk mesh that holds its fine islands in place.

title: Surcoat or Vest
creator: Japan
date: Late Edo Period (1603–1867)/Early Meiji Period (1868–1912), 19th century
medium: Stencil on Japanese paper (probably kozo fiber)
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A Japanese paper stencil, probably of kozo fiber, catalogued with the title Surcoat or Vest.
why: A second Japanese cut-paper stencil for comparing cutting styles and pattern scale.

title: Sarasa
creator: Japan
medium: Cotton, plain weave; stenciled; mordant-dyed; painted
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A piece of Japanese cotton cloth patterned by stenciling, mordant dyeing and painting.
why: Shows the printed result that cut stencils produce on textiles.

title: Bedcover
creator: United States, probably New England or Mid-Atlantic
medium: Cotton, plain weave; stenciled and painted
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: An American cotton bedcover decorated with stenciled and painted motifs.
why: An American example of stenciled textiles, useful for comparing with Japanese work from the same century.

title: Otafuku Throwing Black Beans to Chase Away the Demons on New Year's Eve (Senmen Otafuku zu)
creator: Toshusai Sharaku 東洲斎 写楽 (Japanese, active 1794-95)
medium: Fan print, stencil-printed color on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A fan-shaped Japanese print of Otafuku throwing beans on New Year's Eve, with color printed by stencil.
why: Shows stencil-printed color on a Japanese print rather than on cloth.

title: Kumano of the Hanabishiya as Shiko (Actor Ichikawa Shiko I) Playing Sukehachi (Shiko yaku Sukehachi), from the series Gion Festival
creator: Urakusai Nagahide (Japanese, active c.1805-1848)
medium: Woodblock/stencil print (kappazuri); ink on paper, with stenciled color
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A Kyoto kappazuri print of a festival costume figure, with outlines printed from a block and color added by stencil.
why: Kappazuri combines a printed key line with flat stencil colors, a model for layered stencil prints.

title: Woman's Head with Roses
creator: Koloman (Kolo) Moser (Austrian, 1868-1918)
medium: Color pochoir on paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A color pochoir print on paper of a woman's head with roses.
why: A Vienna Secession pochoir that shows the flat, crisp color areas the technique produces.

title: Poor Pandora!...
creator: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen (French, born Switzerland, 1859-1923)
medium: Lithograph in black with hand-stenciled color (pochoir) in blue, yellow, and orange on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black lithograph with blue, yellow and orange color added by hand stencil.
why: Shows pochoir used to add a few hand-stenciled colors over a black printed drawing.
check: Steinlen illustration. Check the subject is suitable for children before launch.

title: Misery Under the Snow
creator: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen (French, born Switzerland, 1859-1923); printed by Edouard Kleinmann (French, 1844-1927)
medium: Lithograph in black with stenciled colors (green, blue, red and tan) on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A black lithograph of a winter scene with green, blue, red and tan added by stencil.
why: Four stenciled colors over one black drawing show how each color needs its own stencil.
check: Steinlen illustration. Check the subject is suitable for children before launch.

title: Muguette
creator: Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen (French, born Switzerland, 1859-1923)
medium: Lithograph (pen & ink and crayon) in black with stenciled color (slate blue, red, dk brown and black) on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A pen and crayon lithograph in black with slate blue, red, dark brown and black color added by stencil.
why: Another stencil-colored print for comparing how much color an artist chooses to add.

title: The Street Gazette: Grand Inauguration of the New Racetrack Situated on Peñón Hill in Mexico City
creator: José Guadalupe Posada (Mexican, 1852-1913)
medium: Relief engraving or photo relief etching with stenciled color on wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A Mexican broadsheet announcing the opening of a racetrack on Peñón Hill, printed in relief with stenciled color.
why: Shows stencil coloring used on cheap popular prints in Mexico, alongside the French fine-art examples.

title: Panel Entitled "Femme à marguerite" (Woman with Daisy)
creator: Designed by Alphonse Marie Mucha (Czech, 1860–1939); produced by Scheurer Lauth & Cie, Mulhouse, France
medium: Cotton, plain weave; screen printed
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A screen-printed cotton panel of a woman with a daisy, designed by Alphonse Mucha.
why: An early commercial screenprint on fabric from around 1900, long before screenprinting became a fine-art medium.

title: Wurzblatt (Wallpaper Design)
creator: Designed by Dagobert Peche (Austrian, 1887–1923); manufactured by F. O. Schmidt, Vienna
medium: Ink, on paper; screen printed
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A screen-printed wallpaper design in ink on paper by Dagobert Peche.
why: Shows screenprinting used for repeating patterns on paper in the early twentieth century.

title: Sample Book Containing 125 Swatches
creator: Produced by the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna, active 1903–1932)
medium: Silk or wool, plain weave; screen printed
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A sample book of screen-printed silk and wool fabric swatches from the Wiener Werkstätte.
why: A sample book lets students compare many screen-printed patterns and color choices at once.

title: Cigar Ribbon Quilt
creator: United States
medium: Silk, plain weave; screen printed, stenciled, and/or stamped ribbons; pieced and embroidered with silk in feather stitches; underlaid with cotton, warp-float faced 2:1 twill weave and batting; backed with silk, plain weave; machine-stitch quilted with silk
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A silk quilt pieced from cigar ribbons that were screen printed, stenciled or stamped, with embroidered feather stitching.
why: Printed cigar ribbons are an everyday nineteenth-century use of screen and stencil printing that students can recognize as packaging.

title: Le sourire: Journal sérieux, Oct. 13, 1899
creator: Paul Gauguin (French, 1848-1903)
medium: Mimeograph in brownish-black ink, with wood-block prints in black ink on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A page of Gauguin's handmade newspaper Le sourire, with text duplicated by mimeograph and woodblock-printed images in black.
why: An artist using a mimeograph stencil duplicator to publish his own small newspaper.
check: Gauguin's satirical newspaper. Check the page for caricature or nudity before launch.

title: Le sourire: Journal méchant, Mar. 1900
creator: Paul Gauguin (French, 1848-1903)
medium: Mimeograph in brownish-black ink, with wood-block print in black ink on cream wove paper
license: Public domain (CC0), Art Institute of Chicago
alt: A page of Gauguin's newspaper Le sourire, with mimeographed text and a woodblock print in black.
why: A second issue that shows the brownish mimeograph ink next to black woodblock printing on the same sheet.
